content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to adapt frozen vision models for downstream tasks at light cost in terms of parameters and computation. The key idea is to learn a Prompt Generation Network (PGN) designed for generating prompts of every individual input so that prompts are not shared by all different inputs as previous alternatives. The model pipeline is simple. Experiments on 12 datasets show that the proposed method is superior over previous prompt learning methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**
- The writing is clear and easy to follow, and the key details are all given as can see

- The idea of input-dependent visual prompt is interesting and solid, and importantly, effective for a set of downstream tasks.

- The way of using a token library and $K$ mappings for parameter efficiency is valid.

- The overall model design is simple and elegant

- The experiments show that the proposed method is strong in comparison.


**Weakness**

- The input condition concept is not entirely new with prompt learning, which has been attempted in (Zhou et al., 2022b) although using the textual token space. 

- Experiment: 
> 1) For text prompt, [A1] may be a stronger competitor and would be useful to be included in comparison
> 2) It would be also interesting to see the comparison to (Zhou et al., 2022b) that is also input conditioned.

**References**
[A1] Zhou et al. Learning to Prompt for Vision-Language Models. IJCV 2022

The whole paper is written very clearly

The novelty is acceptable although some similar idea exists with some difference

The quality is mostly ok with some improvement in experimental evaluation

It is of good reproducibility.

This is a simple yet effective method with strong results in comparison to previous methods. 

Some downsides including (1) the idea of input conditioning in prompt learning is not significantly novel; (2) more recent prompt learning methods are missing in evaluation.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper mainly focuses on the adaptation of pretrained vision transformers on various downstream tasks. The authors point out that the weaknesses of the previous prompt based methods lie in the limited capacity and the independence of input samples. To solve these problems, the authors propose to use a simple network to composite input-dependent prompt based on a token library. They conduct several experiments to validate the efficacy of this module.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1.	The motivation of using input-dependent prompt is insightful, since most of the previous works concentrate on the usage of fixed form of prompts/prefixes, while omitting the generation of them.


Weaknesses:
1.	The description of the method is not very clear. For example, Eq.(3) uses index $i$ for both visual prompt $\hat{h}$ and images $I_i$. However it seems that $i$ in the LHS denotes the index of prompts (i.e. i=1,2,3,…,K), while the item in the RHS denotes the index of batch sample (i.e. i=1,2,3,…,B). I am not sure if the notations are abused in this equation as well as in Eq.(4). Besides, the structure of the PGN is not clear. The authors mention that they use Res10 as the backbone network of PGN, but it is not explained that how can the output of Res10 be transformed into multiple probability distributions that indicate the composition of each prompt. Are multiple Res10 used in this process, or there is an extra mapping function? 
2.	The authors mention in the introduction that compared with direct finetuning, using prompts can help solve catastrophic forgetting. However there is no experiments in this paper supporting this claim.
3.	Efficiency is one of the most highlighted characteristic of the proposed method, as illustrated in the title. I can barely agree with this point since the size of parameters introduced by the proposed method is about 13 times by the visual prompt, and also much larger than linear fintuning. The improvement as shown in Tab.5 is not surprising when considering the huge amount of parameters.
4.	It seems that in Tab.1 and Tab.5 VP and the proposed PGN share the same number of prompts (K). I am not sure if this is fair enough for comparison. In fact, the proposed method can be seen as an input-dependent masking mechanism on N prompts if the distribution in Eq.(4) is a sharp one. Therefore there is always N alternative prompts that can be used in this model. Using K prompts instead of N in VP definitely has lower capacity, which can possibly lead to worse performance. 
5.	It would be better if the authors could reorganize the space between figures and captions in Fig.3 and Fig.4.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: To enable more efficient foundational model finetuning, this paper aims to empower prompt learning in the vision domain. In particular, it proposes the Prompt Generation Network (PGN) to generate input-dependent prompts for each given image via sampling from a learned library of tokens. The experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed method in greatly reducing trainable parameters while maintaining similar finetuning accuracy as compared to whole model finetuning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

1. Among the early works that introduce prompt learning to the vision domain, it is good to see its cross-domain effectiveness.

2. This paper provides extensive experiments and the visualization and qualitative analysis can enhance the understanding of visual prompts.

**Weakness**

1. The major concern of this paper is the limited novelty. The effectiveness of input-dependent prompts has been validated in the NLP domain [1] and the vision domain [2], both of which adopt prompt pools that are similar with the proposed learned token library in this paper. Considering prompt learning has already been validated to be effectiveness in [3][4], it is not surprise or very interesting to see input-dependent prompts can further improve the finetuning accuracy.

2. The evaluation results in Table 5 seem to indicate that the proposed PGN often has a similar or even lower accuracy with linear finetuning. Does this indicate visual prompts are marginally useful as compared to conventional linear finetuning? In addition, is there any insight why the accuracy rankings between PGN and linear finetuning are very dataset-specific?

3. A missing visual prompt baseline is [4]. In addition, finetuning on more tasks like object detection and segmentation via visual prompt tuning can greatly strengthen the experiments.


Minors:

(1) Typos: Abstract "Prompt leaning" => "Prompt learning"


Reference:

[1] "Attentional Mixtures of Soft Prompt Tuning for Parameter-efficient Multi-task Knowledge Sharing". A. Asai et al., EMNLP 2022.

[2] "Learning to Prompt for Continual Learning", Z. Wang et al., CVPR 2022.

[3] "Visual Prompt Tuning", M. Jia et al., ECCV 2022.

[4] "Neural Prompt Search", Y. Zhang et al., arXiv 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper shows good clarity but suffers from limited novelty, considering similar prompt learning schemes have been explored in both NLP and vision domains. For the reproducibility, the authors promise to open-source codes once published.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to the major concern of limited novelty and contributions over previous (visual) prompt tuning methods, the paper is marginally below the acceptance threshold. I'm willing to adjust my scores if the concerns are properly addressed.
